extracted.intended_audience: U.S. design patent applicants, in-house counsel, and IP practitioners considering international design protection
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on using the Hague International Design System (WIPO) to obtain design patent protection in multiple countries, covering filing routes, application content limits, WIPO formalities review, national examination/refusal procedures, term/renewal, and central management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial nature of design patent protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patent protection is territorial — to secure protection in a particular country or jurisdiction, one must file a design patent in each country or jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose filing route (direct or via Hague) depending on which countries/jurisdictions you want protection in and whether they are Hague contracting parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct versus indirect filing routes
rubrics_metrics.description: Two ways to obtain foreign protection: file directly with each foreign intellectual property office (requiring foreign associates) or file indirectly via the Hague International Design System (single international application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before the U.S. joined Hague in 2015, only direct filings were available to U.S. entities. Use direct filing for non-Hague countries or when local counsel assistance is required; use Hague to streamline filings across multiple Hague members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hague membership limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hague route only covers member countries/jurisdictions; there are currently 75 contracting parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If protection is desired in countries not signatory to the Hague Agreement, the applicant must file directly in those countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design count and Locarno classification requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A Hague international design application allows the inclusion of up to 100 designs in one application, provided the designs all belong in the same Locarno classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group related designs under the same Locarno class to maximize efficiency; otherwise separate applications are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproductions (views) format and number
rubrics_metrics.description: Each design may include multiple views (called reproductions). The reproductions can be lined drawings or photographs, may be black and white or in color, and can include both types in one application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sufficient views to depict the design clearly and comply with formal requirements of WIPO and potential designated offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost drivers for Hague international design application
rubrics_metrics.description: The cost of filing a Hague international design application depends on the number of countries or jurisdictions designated, which country or jurisdiction is designated, the number of designs, and the number of reproductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budgeting should account for per-design and per-designation fees; Hague can be cost-effective especially when multiple designs and many designated countries are involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority claims and U.S. filing not required
rubrics_metrics.description: A Hague international design application can claim priority to an earlier filed U.S. design patent application, but it is not necessary to first file a U.S. design patent application (unlike the Madrid trademark system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether to file a U.S. priority application before filing Hague, depending on filing strategy and priority benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: WIPO formalities review and Notices of Irregularities
rubrics_metrics.description: After filing, WIPO reviews the application for compliance with formalities. If WIPO determines non-compliance, it will issue a Notice of Irregularities and typically provide three (3) months to correct any irregularities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare applications carefully to avoid irregularities and the need for corrections; timely responses to Notices of Irregularities are required to proceed to registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: International Registration Certificate and publication timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: If the application is compliant, WIPO will issue an International Registration Certificate. WIPO will also publish the International Registration in the International Designs Bulletin, typically 6 months after filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An International Registration Certificate can issue quickly (as little as a month) if all is in order; expect publication around six months which triggers national examination periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: National examination differences (substantive vs formalities-only)
rubrics_metrics.description: After publication by WIPO, each designated country/jurisdiction reviews the design(s) and decides whether they meet domestic requirements. Some countries will substantively examine unity, novelty, etc. (e.g., U.S., Canada), while others will review on formalities only (e.g., European Union).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate different substantive standards and prepare to respond to objections where substantive examination occurs; work with local counsel to address country-specific issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal period and response procedure for designated countries
rubrics_metrics.description: A country or jurisdiction must issue a refusal within 6 months (in some instances 12 months) of publication of the International Registration and notify WIPO. A response must be filed directly with the country's or jurisdiction's intellectual property office to overcome a refusal, typically requiring a foreign associate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor national deadlines closely and engage local counsel promptly to respond to refusals; failure to respond can result in loss of protection in that country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Granting, Statement of Grant, and deemed protection
rubrics_metrics.description: If a country or jurisdiction approves the design(s), it may explicitly issue a Statement of Grant and notify WIPO. For certain countries, a Statement of Grant is issued for each design along with the country's own Certificate of Registration and/or Registration number. A country is not required to issue a Statement of Grant and if no refusal is issued within the 6 (or 12) month period, protection is deemed to be granted automatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume uniform issuance of national certificates—check WIPO notices and national registers to confirm protection status in each designated country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term of international registration and renewals
rubrics_metrics.description: An International Registration is effective in countries that grant protection or do not timely refuse. The initial term of the International Registration is five (5) years from the filing date. It may be renewed at least twice for a term of fifteen (15) years, and for certain countries or jurisdictions, for a maximum term of twenty-five (25) years (e.g., Europe, Japan). Renewal is done centrally via WIPO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track renewal windows and renewal rules per-designation since maximum terms can vary by jurisdiction; use WIPO's central renewal mechanism for convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralized post-registration management via WIPO
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignment and change of address can also be done centrally via WIPO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use central procedures to record ownership changes and contact updates to simplify global portfolio management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical recommendation to maximize Hague benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hague International Design System can be a very cost effective way to protect designs in multiple countries, especially when there are multiple designs involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To maximize benefits, ensure the application is properly filed to minimize the possibility of refusal by a designated country or jurisdiction—careful drafting, correct classification, and adequate reproductions reduce downstream problems.
